title: Understand TLS and HTTPS
where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: Think of HTTPS as a protected delivery envelope for HTTP messages.
TLS encrypts traffic in transit, checks that messages were not changed, and helps the client authenticate the endpoint when it validates the certificate.
SSL is the older protocol family; people still say SSL certificate, but this lab uses TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, not SSL, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1.
HTTPS does not prove an application has no bugs or that every person using it is authorized.
expected: Your notes say TLS protects the connection; HTTPS is HTTP carried over that connection.
output: Your notes say TLS protects the connection; HTTPS is HTTP carried over that connection.

title: Meet the public certificate and secret key
where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: Think of a certificate as a school ID card showing a name, an issuer and an expiry date. The real certificate also contains a public key.
Think of the private key as the secret way the server proves it owns that public key. It is not copied into the certificate.
A TLS handshake uses cryptography to prove possession and establish shared traffic keys. Do not imagine the public certificate itself is a secret password.
If a private key is exposed, treat it as an incident: replace it and follow revocation policy. Merely changing its filename is not a fix.
expected: Your notes have PUBLIC: certificate and CSR; SECRET: website private key and CA private keys.
output: Your notes have PUBLIC: certificate and CSR; SECRET: website private key and CA private keys.

title: Meet the CSR and signing office
where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: A Certificate Signing Request, or CSR, is an application form containing a public key and requested names.
It is signed using the matching private key so the CA can check the request was not changed. That signature does not prove your organization owns the requested domain.
A certificate authority, or CA, checks identity and authority using its own policy, then may issue a signed certificate.
Our simulated CA follows a small practice approval checklist. It is not connected to DoD or a public CA.
expected: You can put the sequence in order: key → CSR → approval → signed certificate.
output: You can put the sequence in order: key → CSR → approval → signed certificate.

title: Build the trust chain
where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: The website leaf certificate is like your ID. An intermediate CA is the office allowed to issue it. A root CA is the top trust anchor.
The root signs the intermediate; the intermediate signs the website certificate. The root private key is especially sensitive and normally kept offline in a real PKI.
NGINX sends the website certificate first, then the intermediate certificates in order. It normally does not send the root.
The client separately decides which roots to trust. Receiving a root from a random website does not make it trusted.
expected: Your drawn chain is leaf → intermediate → trusted root. Your server bundle is leaf + intermediate, not key + root.
output: Your drawn chain is leaf → intermediate → trusted root. Your server bundle is leaf + intermediate, not key + root.

title: Check names, dates and matching keys
where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: The Subject Alternative Name, or SAN, must include app.example.mil. Modern clients check SANs; the Common Name alone is not enough.
The current time must be within notBefore and notAfter. Expired certificates cause clients to reject the connection, even if NGINX still runs.
The certificate’s public key must match the private key used by NGINX. We compare public-key fingerprints without displaying secret key data.
We also check issuer chain, server-auth purpose and local policy. A good date alone is not a complete check.
expected: Your checklist includes name, time, trusted chain, permitted purpose and matching private key.
output: Your checklist includes name, time, trusted chain, permitted purpose and matching private key.

prompt = no

req_extensions = req_ext
[dn]
CN = app.example.mil
[req_ext]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
[alt_names]

basicConstraints = critical,CA:TRUE,pathlen:0
keyUsage = critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign
subjectKeyIdentifier = hash
authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid,issuer
EOF
